questions.stem: In the stimulus-response model, what is the role of the control centre?
options: It carries out the response that returns a condition towards normal
It produces the stimulus that begins the response in the organism
It receives information from receptors and sends instructions to effectors
It detects a change in the internal or external environment of the organism
questions.explanation: Receptors detect the stimulus, the control centre (often in the brain, such as the hypothalamus) processes the information, and effectors such as muscles and glands carry out the response.

questions.stem: Blood glucose rises after a meal, insulin is released, and blood glucose falls back towards normal, so less insulin is released. What kind of control is this?
options: Positive feedback, because the response increases the original change
A reflex, because it involves only the nervous system and the spinal cord
Tolerance, because the body allows glucose to stay outside its normal range
Negative feedback, because the response reverses the original change
questions.explanation: In negative feedback the response counteracts the stimulus, and as the condition returns to normal the response decreases. Positive feedback would push glucose further from normal.

questions.stem: During childbirth, contractions push the baby against the cervix, which triggers release of oxytocin, which causes stronger contractions. Why is this not homeostasis?
options: It involves a hormone, and homeostasis only ever uses nervous pathways
It involves muscles as effectors, and homeostasis only ever uses glands as effectors
It is positive feedback, which amplifies a change instead of keeping conditions stable
It is negative feedback, which reverses a change instead of keeping conditions stable
questions.explanation: Each step increases the stimulus, so the change grows until the baby is born; that is positive feedback. Homeostasis uses negative feedback to hold conditions near a set point, through nervous and hormonal pathways and any effector.

questions.stem: In vertebrates, how are receptors and effectors linked to the control centre?
options: By nervous pathways, hormonal pathways, or both working together
By nervous pathways only, since hormones act only within one cell
By hormonal pathways only, since nerves cannot reach every effector
By direct contact, since receptors and effectors are the same cells
questions.explanation: Information travels as nerve impulses along neurons or as hormones in the blood, and many responses, such as thermoregulation, use both. The two pathways often act together.

questions.stem: A person's blood becomes more concentrated after sweating. The hypothalamus detects this, the pituitary releases a hormone, and the kidneys reabsorb more water. Identify the receptor and the effector.
options: Receptor: the sweat glands. Effector: the pituitary gland's hormone cells
Receptor: the pituitary gland. Effector: the sweat glands in the skin
Receptor: osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus. Effector: the kidney tubules
Receptor: the kidney tubules. Effector: osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus
questions.explanation: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the rise in solute concentration, and the kidney tubules respond by reabsorbing more water. The pituitary is part of the pathway, releasing the hormone that carries the message.

questions.stem: Which comparison of nervous and hormonal pathways is correct?
options: Nervous messages travel in the blood; hormonal messages travel along the axons of neurons
Nervous messages reach every cell in the body; hormonal messages reach only one target cell
Nervous responses are faster and shorter lived; hormonal responses are slower and last longer
Nervous responses are slower and last longer; hormonal responses are faster and shorter lived
questions.explanation: Impulses travel along neurons in milliseconds to specific effectors, and the effect stops quickly. Hormones travel in the blood, take longer to act and their effects often last longer.

questions.stem: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) causes the thyroid to release thyroxine, and high thyroxine levels reduce TSH release. What would you expect if the thyroid were removed and no thyroxine given?
options: Thyroxine levels would rise, because TSH would act on other glands instead
TSH levels would rise, because thyroxine no longer inhibits its release
TSH levels would fall, because the thyroid no longer stimulates its release
TSH levels would stay the same, because TSH is controlled only by temperature
questions.explanation: Thyroxine normally exerts negative feedback on TSH release. With no thyroxine, the brake is removed and TSH rises, even though there is no gland left to respond to it.

questions.stem: What is meant by an organism's tolerance limits?
options: The highest number of offspring the organism can raise each year
The largest population of the species that a habitat can support
The time an organism can survive after its homeostasis has failed
The range of a condition within which the organism can survive
questions.explanation: Each organism can survive only within a certain range of factors such as temperature and water availability. Outside that range, homeostasis fails and the organism is stressed or dies. The largest population a habitat supports is its carrying capacity.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a behavioural response that helps an animal stay within its tolerance limits?
options: A seal having a thick layer of blubber under its skin
A dog's heart rate rising when it begins to run
A bird's feathers growing thicker before winter
A lizard basking in the sun in the early morning
questions.explanation: Behavioural responses are actions, such as moving into the sun or shade. Blubber and thicker feathers are structural features, and a rising heart rate is a physiological change.

questions.stem: Some small marsupials enter torpor on cold nights, lowering their body temperature and metabolic rate for some hours. What type of change is this, and what does it achieve?
options: A structural change that adds insulation so less heat is lost in the cold
A behavioural change that brings the animal into warmer surroundings at night
A metabolic change that raises body temperature by burning extra food
A metabolic change that saves energy when food is scarce and heat loss is high
questions.explanation: Torpor is a controlled drop in metabolic rate and body temperature. Keeping a high body temperature in the cold costs a small animal a great deal of energy, so torpor saves energy until conditions improve.

questions.stem: A frog can survive water temperatures of 5 to 30 degrees C, but it grows and breeds only between 15 and 25 degrees C. What do these data show?
options: The frog will breed faster as the water warms, up to the limit of 30 degrees C
Its tolerance range is wider than its optimal range, where it grows and breeds
The frog's tolerance range is 15 to 25 degrees C, since that is where it breeds
The frog can live indefinitely at 5 degrees C, since it survives at that temperature
questions.explanation: The full range, from 5 to 30 degrees C, is its tolerance range, but near the limits the frog survives under stress without growing or breeding. Its optimal range is 15 to 25 degrees C.

questions.stem: In a reflex arc, which neuron carries impulses from the receptor to the central nervous system?
options: Interneuron
Effector neuron
Sensory neuron
Motor neuron
questions.explanation: Sensory neurons carry impulses from receptors to the spinal cord or brain. Interneurons link neurons within the central nervous system, and motor neurons carry impulses out to effectors.

questions.stem: A person steps on a sharp object and pulls the foot away before feeling pain. Why is the response so fast?
options: The brain processes the pain first, then sends a faster signal down the spinal cord
The pathway passes through the spinal cord, without waiting for the brain to process it
The impulse travels in the blood to the leg muscles, which is the fastest route available
The receptor in the foot contracts the leg muscles directly, with no neurons involved
questions.explanation: A reflex arc links sensory neuron, interneuron and motor neuron in the spinal cord, so the response begins before signals reach the brain and pain is felt. Nerve impulses, not blood, carry the message.

questions.stem: What is the approximate resting membrane potential of a typical neuron?
options: 0 mV
-7 mV
-70 mV
+40 mV
questions.explanation: At rest the inside of the axon is about 70 mV negative relative to the outside. During an action potential it briefly rises to about +40 mV before returning.

questions.stem: Which ion movement causes the rising phase (depolarisation) of an action potential?
options: Potassium ions flowing into the axon
Sodium ions pumped out of the axon
Chloride ions flowing out of the axon
Sodium ions flowing into the axon
questions.explanation: When the membrane reaches threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium ions rush in, making the inside positive. Potassium ions then flow out, repolarising the membrane.

questions.stem: What is the role of the sodium-potassium pump in a neuron?
options: It uses ATP to move sodium out and potassium in, maintaining the resting gradients
It lets sodium flow in by diffusion whenever a stimulus reaches the threshold level
It releases neurotransmitter from the axon terminal into the synaptic cleft
It breaks down neurotransmitter in the cleft so the signal does not continue
questions.explanation: The pump actively transports three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in per ATP, keeping the concentration gradients that the action potential relies on. Sodium flowing in at threshold passes through voltage-gated channels, not the pump.

questions.stem: Why can a neuron not fire a second action potential immediately after the first?
options: During the refractory period, sodium channels cannot reopen straight away
The axon has run out of sodium ions and must make more before firing
The neurotransmitter must first be returned to the cell body of the neuron
The myelin sheath must reform around the axon after each action potential
questions.explanation: After opening, voltage-gated sodium channels are inactivated for a short time, so the membrane cannot respond. This refractory period also makes impulses travel in one direction along the axon.

questions.stem: Stronger stimuli do not produce larger action potentials. How does the nervous system tell a strong stimulus from a weak one?
options: A stronger stimulus produces action potentials more frequently
A stronger stimulus produces action potentials that travel slower
A stronger stimulus produces action potentials with a negative peak
A stronger stimulus produces one action potential that lasts longer
questions.explanation: Action potentials are all-or-none and always the same size. Intensity is coded by how often they fire, and by how many neurons are activated.

questions.stem: When an action potential reaches the axon terminal, which event causes neurotransmitter to be released?
options: Neurotransmitter diffuses straight through the membrane of the terminal
Calcium ions enter the terminal, causing vesicles to fuse with the membrane
Sodium ions leave the terminal, causing the vesicles to burst open inside
Potassium ions enter the terminal, dissolving the membrane of the terminal
questions.explanation: Depolarisation opens calcium channels; calcium entry triggers vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter by exocytosis into the synaptic cleft.

questions.stem: What is meant by signal transduction at a synapse?
options: Turning neurotransmitter binding into a response in the next cell
Converting an electrical impulse into heat energy in the synaptic cleft
Converting the neurotransmitter into a hormone that enters the blood
Converting a motor neuron into a sensory neuron as the signal passes
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitter binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, which opens ion channels or starts a chain of reactions inside the cell, so the chemical signal becomes a new electrical or chemical response.

questions.stem: An insecticide blocks the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, which normally breaks down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft. What effect would this have on muscles?
options: They would contract continuously, because the neurotransmitter keeps stimulating them
They would fail to contract, because no neurotransmitter is released into the cleft
They would relax permanently, because the receptors are destroyed by the insecticide
They would be unaffected, because the enzyme acts only in the central nervous system
questions.explanation: Without the enzyme, acetylcholine stays bound to receptors and keeps stimulating the muscle cells, causing prolonged contraction and spasms. Release of the neurotransmitter is not affected.

questions.stem: How does the way a steroid hormone acts on a target cell differ from the way a protein hormone acts?
options: A steroid hormone crosses the membrane and binds an internal receptor; a protein hormone binds a membrane receptor
A steroid hormone binds a membrane receptor; a protein hormone crosses the membrane and binds an internal receptor
A steroid hormone acts on every cell in the body; a protein hormone acts only on cells of the nervous system
A steroid hormone is carried along neurons; a protein hormone is carried dissolved in the blood plasma
questions.explanation: Lipid-soluble steroids diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer and bind receptors inside the cell, often affecting gene transcription. Protein hormones cannot cross the membrane, so they bind surface receptors that trigger signal transduction inside the cell.

questions.stem: What is an endotherm?
options: An animal whose body temperature always matches the temperature of its surroundings
An animal that gains most of its body heat by basking in sunlight during the day
An animal that lives only in warm climates, where it gains heat from its environment
An animal that keeps its body temperature up mainly with metabolic heat
questions.explanation: Endotherms, such as mammals and birds, generate heat by metabolism and regulate their core temperature within narrow limits. Animals that rely mainly on outside heat sources are ectotherms.

questions.stem: A person moves from a warm room into the cold. Which response is controlled by the hypothalamus to reduce heat loss?
options: Constriction of arterioles supplying the skin
Dilation of arterioles supplying the skin
Increased secretion from the sweat glands
Faster breathing to release warm air
questions.explanation: Vasoconstriction diverts blood away from the skin surface, reducing heat lost by radiation and conduction. Vasodilation and sweating increase heat loss.

questions.stem: Arteries carrying warm blood to a penguin's feet run right beside veins carrying cold blood back. What is the advantage of this arrangement?
options: Heat passes from venous to arterial blood, so the feet stay as warm as the body core
Blood mixes between the arteries and veins, so the feet receive extra oxygen
The cold veins cool the arteries, so the bird's core temperature falls to save energy
Heat passes from arterial to venous blood, so less heat reaches the feet and is lost
questions.explanation: This countercurrent heat exchanger transfers heat to the returning blood before it reaches the feet, so the feet stay cool and little heat is lost to the ice, while the core stays warm.

questions.stem: Desert-dwelling mammals often have larger ears than related species from cold regions. How does this help?
options: A large ear reduces the animal's surface area, so less water is lost by sweating
A large ear surface with many blood vessels increases heat loss to the air
A large ear traps a layer of still air that insulates the animal's head
A large ear collects more sunlight, warming the animal on cold desert nights
questions.explanation: Large, thin, well-supplied ears add surface area for radiating heat, a structural feature useful in hot climates. Cold-climate relatives tend to have smaller extremities, which reduces heat loss.

questions.stem: How does shivering help an endotherm maintain its body temperature in the cold?
options: Rapid muscle contractions raise the hairs, which reflect heat back in
Rapid muscle contractions reduce metabolic rate, which conserves energy
Rapid muscle contractions increase respiration, which releases heat
Rapid muscle contractions push warm blood to the surface of the skin
questions.explanation: Shivering is involuntary contraction of skeletal muscles; the extra respiration needed releases heat. Raising hairs is a separate response that traps an insulating layer of air.

questions.stem: In prolonged cold, the hypothalamus causes extra thyroxine to be released. How does this help maintain body temperature?
options: It triggers shivering in skeletal muscle within a fraction of a second
It lowers the set point, so a lower body temperature is accepted
It raises the metabolic rate of body cells, so more heat is produced
It constricts the skin arterioles, so less heat is lost from the surface
questions.explanation: Thyroxine increases the metabolic rate of most cells, so they release more heat; this hormonal response is slower but longer lasting than nervous responses such as vasoconstriction and shivering.

questions.stem: Dogs have few sweat glands. How do they increase heat loss on a hot day?
options: By fluffing up their fur to trap a layer of warm air
By panting, which evaporates water from the mouth and airways
By shivering, which uses up heat stored in the muscles
By constricting arterioles in the skin to keep heat inside
questions.explanation: Panting moves air rapidly over moist surfaces of the tongue and airways, and evaporation removes heat. Constricting skin arterioles and fluffing fur reduce heat loss.

questions.stem: What is the difference between an osmoregulator and an osmoconformer?
options: An osmoregulator has no kidneys; an osmoconformer uses kidneys to control water
An osmoregulator controls its internal solute concentration; an osmoconformer matches its surroundings
An osmoregulator matches its surroundings; an osmoconformer controls its internal solute concentration
An osmoregulator lives only in fresh water; an osmoconformer lives only on land
questions.explanation: Osmoregulators keep their body fluids at a steady concentration whatever the surroundings; osmoconformers, such as many marine invertebrates, let their body fluids match the surrounding seawater.

questions.stem: Many marine invertebrates, such as sea stars, are osmoconformers. Why is this possible for them but not for a freshwater animal?
options: Freshwater animals have no cell membranes, so osmosis cannot affect their cells
Fresh water is more concentrated than body fluids, so it would draw salts in
Seawater is about as concentrated as their body fluids; fresh water is far more dilute
Seawater contains no salts, so their cells neither gain nor lose water by osmosis
questions.explanation: Body fluids matching seawater do not upset cell function. Fresh water is so dilute that conforming to it would leave cells with too few solutes to work, so freshwater animals must osmoregulate.

questions.stem: A freshwater fish lives in water that is far more dilute than its body fluids. How does it maintain water balance?
options: It drinks large amounts of water and actively excretes salts through its gills
It produces small volumes of concentrated urine and avoids drinking any water
It allows its body fluids to become as dilute as the surrounding fresh water
It makes large volumes of dilute urine and actively absorbs salts at its gills
questions.explanation: Water enters by osmosis across the gills, so the fish gets rid of it as copious dilute urine and replaces lost salts by active uptake at the gills. Drinking and excreting salt is what a marine bony fish does.

questions.stem: A marine bony fish has body fluids more dilute than seawater. Which set of responses maintains its water balance?
options: It avoids drinking, allows its fluids to match seawater and produces no urine
It drinks seawater, excretes excess salt through its gills and produces little urine
It avoids drinking, absorbs salt through its gills and produces a lot of dilute urine
It drinks seawater, absorbs more salt through its gills and produces a lot of urine
questions.explanation: The fish loses water by osmosis to the salty sea, so it drinks seawater, actively pumps the extra salt out through its gills and conserves water by producing small amounts of urine.

questions.stem: Some Australian desert rodents can survive without drinking. Which feature best explains this?
options: Sweat glands that release large volumes of water for cooling
Thin fur that lets water evaporate quickly from the skin
Activity in the hottest part of the day to find food quickly
Kidneys that produce very concentrated urine, conserving water
questions.explanation: Long loops of Henle let these animals reabsorb most water from their filtrate and excrete very concentrated urine; they also obtain water from food and metabolism and avoid daytime heat by sheltering in burrows.

questions.stem: Which feature helps a plant in a dry habitat reduce water loss?
options: Stomata sunken in pits in the leaf surface
Large, thin leaves with many surface stomata
A thin cuticle over the upper leaf surface
Shallow roots that spread under the surface
questions.explanation: Sunken stomata trap humid air above the pore, reducing the concentration gradient for water vapour and so slowing transpiration. Large thin leaves with many exposed stomata increase water loss.

questions.stem: Some desert plants open their stomata only at night, storing carbon dioxide as an acid and using it for photosynthesis during the day. What is the main advantage?
options: More oxygen is absorbed, because respiration is fastest at night
Less carbon dioxide is needed, because the plant stops respiring by day
Less water is lost, because stomata open when it is cool and humid
More light is captured, because photosynthesis can happen in darkness
questions.explanation: Opening stomata in the cool night air greatly reduces water lost by transpiration, while stored carbon dioxide still allows photosynthesis in daylight with stomata closed. Light reactions still need light.

questions.stem: Grey mangroves grow in salty tidal mud. How do some mangroves maintain water balance in such a salty environment?
options: They excrete excess salt through glands on their leaves
They absorb salt freely and store it in their xylem
They take in seawater through stomata on their leaves
They lower their root solute concentration below seawater
questions.explanation: Some mangroves, such as the grey mangrove, secrete salt from glands on their leaves, while others exclude much of the salt at the roots. Keeping their root cells more concentrated than seawater lets them still take up water.

questions.stem: When soil water runs low, a plant's roots produce a hormone that travels to the leaves and causes the stomata to close. What type of response is this?
options: A positive feedback response that increases transpiration further
A homeostatic, physiological response that reduces water loss
A structural response that permanently thickens the leaf cuticle
A behavioural response in which the plant moves to wetter soil
questions.explanation: Plants also use stimulus-response pathways: the root detects water shortage and a hormonal signal triggers guard cells to close the stomata, reducing transpiration. It is reversible, not a permanent structural change.
